author: Olympiodorus of Alexandria
occasion: A brief exegetical or paraenetic fragment on the command to rejoice in the day of persecution, explaining why suffering for the truth is itself a reward and a cause of joy.
argument: Olympiodorus argues that just as a healthy and robust person takes pleasure even before luxury, having pleasure allotted together with health, so spiritual health brings joy even amid suffering. Paul rejoiced in his sufferings not only because of the kingdom of heaven, in which a prize is set for virtue, but also in the very suffering, since this too is the greatest prize, to suffer something for the truth. The apostles rejoiced after being dishonored for the name of Jesus, since this very thing, even by itself, is the greatest honor and crown and prize and source of unfading pleasure. The contest of slander is declared to be not small but very great, and Solomon's words are cited to illustrate the harshness of the contest: he saw the slanders that occur under the sun, and the tear of the slandered, and there was no one to comfort them. Since the contest is great, the crown laid up for it is greater, and Christ commands those who contend in this contest to rejoice and leap for joy with fitting endurance.

outline.move: A comparison from bodily health introduces the principle that the healthy and robust person takes pleasure even before luxury, having pleasure allotted together with health, and Paul is cited as rejoicing in his sufferings.

scripture: The fragment quotes Paul and Solomon without formal citations. Paul's words echo Colossians 1:24 and the apostles' rejoicing reflects Acts 5:41. Solomon's words are from Ecclesiastes 4:1. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names: Colossians, Acts, Ecclesiastes.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The original addressee or audience is not stated in the fragment.
The precise biblical source of Paul's quoted words is not explicitly identified in the text.
